notes.meaning: God tells Joshua not to be afraid because Israel had put away the sin of Achan. Now that the Lord's favor had returned, He promised that the king, people, city, and land of Ai were already given into Joshua's hand. God also instructed him to take the entire army, which helped restore the courage of the people after their earlier defeat.

Ai was to be destroyed like Jericho, but this time God allowed the Israelites to keep the livestock and goods for themselves. God also told Joshua to set a hidden ambush behind the city. This showed that God often works through ordinary wisdom and battle plans alongside His miraculous power.

Joshua acted promptly on God's word and gathered the army to march toward Ai. He chose thirty thousand skilled warriors and sent them out secretly under the cover of night. Their goal was to move into position behind the city before daybreak without being noticed.

Joshua gave strict orders to the ambush force to hide behind the city on the west side and not wander too far away. They had to stay quiet and stay on guard. When the right moment came, they needed to be ready to strike quickly.

Joshua explained the battle strategy to the troops who stayed with him. He and the main force would march directly toward the city walls to draw the enemy out. When the soldiers of Ai attacked as they had in the first battle, the Israelites would pretend to be scared and run away.

The purpose of running away was to lure the enemy far outside the protection of their fortress. Joshua knew the king of Ai would be proud and confident because of his previous victory. That pride would trick the defenders into leaving their city completely unguarded.

Once the men of Ai had chased the main force away from the walls, the hidden troops were ordered to jump up and seize the empty city. Joshua reminded them that their victory would come from the Lord their God, who had promised to deliver it into their hands.

As soon as the ambush captured the city, they were commanded to set parts of it on fire. The rising column of smoke would serve as a signal to Joshua and the retreating army that the trap had succeeded. Joshua reminded them to follow God's commands with care.

Joshua sent the ambush unit to their hidden post between Bethel and Ai, to the west of the city. He then spent the night in the camp among the main body of his soldiers. Staying with the people showed that he shared their risks and gave them confidence.

Joshua rose early in the morning and inspected his soldiers to make sure every unit was in order. He and the elders of Israel then led the army toward Ai. The elders accompanied him as respected leaders to represent the nation and help oversee the division of the plunder.

Joshua marched the main army right up in front of Ai and made camp on the north side of the city. A valley lay between the Israelite camp and the town walls. This placed the Israelite troops in plain sight of the Canaanite defenders.

Joshua stationed about five thousand men to hide to the west between Bethel and Ai. This detachment lay in wait in the rocky ground to rush the town as soon as the defenders moved out. They were positioned close enough to act quickly while staying hidden from view.

The troops were now positioned with the main army to the north and the ambush to the west. During the night, Joshua went down into the middle of the valley. He likely went there to inspect the ground and pray for God's blessing before the battle began.

When the king of Ai saw the Israelites in the morning, he rushed his soldiers out to fight them in the open plain. He was confident of an easy victory because he had won before. In his haste and overconfidence, he had no idea an ambush was waiting behind his city.

When the two armies met, Joshua and his men acted as if they were losing and fled toward the wilderness. This pretend retreat made the enemy believe the Israelites were terrified again. It took strong discipline for the soldiers to fall back on purpose.

All the fighting men in Ai were called out to chase down the retreating Israelites. In their eagerness to destroy their enemies, they pursued Joshua far into the desert. This reckless pursuit pulled them completely away from the safety of their city.

Not a single soldier remained behind in Ai, and allied troops from nearby Bethel joined the chase as well. Both cities were left completely open and unguarded. Their blind confidence led directly to their destruction.

The Lord told Joshua to stretch out his spear toward Ai, promising to give the city to him. Joshua held up his weapon, which likely carried a pennant or banner visible from a distance. This act served as both a battle signal to the ambush and a sign of God's presence and help.

The moment Joshua held out his spear, the hidden soldiers rose quickly from their hiding places and charged into Ai. Finding the gates open, they captured the town without resistance and immediately set fires. The smoke signaled to Joshua that the plan had worked.

When the men of Ai looked back, they saw dark smoke pouring into the sky from their burning homes. Terrified and confused, they realized they had fallen into a trap and had nowhere to run. At that moment, the Israelites who had been running away stopped, turned around, and attacked.

Seeing the smoke rise, Joshua and his troops knew that their fellow soldiers had captured the city. They turned back in full force and struck down their pursuers. The hunters had suddenly become the hunted.

The ambush party poured out of the city gates and attacked the enemy from the rear. The men of Ai were trapped between the two Israelite forces on both sides. Israel struck them down completely until not a single enemy soldier escaped.

During the fighting, the king of Ai was captured alive and brought directly to Joshua. He was spared in the middle of battle so he could face a formal, public sentence. This ensured his punishment served as a visible warning to all the surrounding nations.

After the army finished destroying the Canaanite soldiers in the open country, they marched back into the city of Ai. They put the remaining population to the sword, carrying out God's judgment against the corrupt inhabitants. Israel acted here as the ministers of God's justice.

A total of twelve thousand people from Ai fell that day, including men and women. The entire city was placed under the ban, which was God's sacred command to completely destroy a wicked population. This brought full judgment on the city that had opposed the Lord.

Joshua kept his hand and spear raised until the battle was completely finished and all the inhabitants were destroyed. Just as Moses held up his hands during battle in Exodus, Joshua maintained this posture to keep the people looking to God for victory. He did not quit until the work commanded by the Lord was done.

Unlike Jericho, where everything was devoted to destruction, the Israelites were allowed to keep the cattle and plunder for themselves. They gathered and shared the spoils under the direction of their leaders. This rewarded Israel's obedience and met the practical needs of the people.

Joshua burned Ai and turned it into a permanent mound of rubble. The city was left ruined as an enduring monument to God's judgment against wicked nations. The desolate site remained a visible witness to future generations of Israel's victory through God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern archaeologists point out that excavations at et-Tell show no occupied city during Joshua's time, leading some scholars to argue that the story was written later to explain an already existing ruin.

notes.meaning: Joshua ordered the king of Ai hanged on a tree to demonstrate God's curse upon wicked leaders. At sunset, his body was taken down in obedience to the law of Moses, which forbade leaving a corpse on a tree overnight. They threw the body by the city gate and piled stones over it as a lasting symbol of disgrace.

After the victory at Ai, Joshua led the people north to Mount Ebal to build an altar to the Lord. Even though the conquest was just beginning, he paused military operations to put God's worship first. This fulfilled the explicit instructions Moses had given for entering the land.

The altar was made of uncut, natural stones without the touch of an iron tool, following the law of Moses. God wanted His worship to remain pure and simple, untouched by human craft. On this altar, the people presented burnt offerings to dedicate themselves to God and peace offerings to celebrate fellowship with Him.

Joshua wrote a copy of the law of Moses onto stones in the presence of all Israel. These stones were likely coated with plaster so the words could be clearly read by everyone. This gave the nation a visible, public record of the standard by which they were called to live.

The entire nation stood in two groups around the ark of the covenant, with half the tribes in front of Mount Gerizim and half in front of Mount Ebal. The priests held the ark in the valley between the hills while the leaders, citizens, and resident foreigners took their places. They assembled just as Moses had directed, ready to hear the covenant blessings.

Joshua read all the words of the law aloud to the assembly, including the blessings for obedience and the curses for disobedience. The people voiced their agreement to the terms of God's covenant. This reminded them that their future prosperity in the land depended entirely on staying faithful to the Lord.

Joshua did not leave out a single word of what Moses had commanded, reading the entire law to the whole gathering. Women, children, and foreigners were all present to hear and learn God's commands. This showed that God's covenant was meant for every member of the community, young and old alike.
